newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turks see $2 billion foreign borrowing in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Turks see $2 billion foreign borrowing in 1997.

text.p: Turkey, confident that its sub-investment credit rating will not fall this year, is planning to raise some $2 billion in international capital markets this year after $2.9 billion last year, officials said.
"We plan to borrow some $2 billion this year mainly in mark, dollar and yen," said a government official who declined to be named.
Officials say the borrowing target might be revised up later in this year in line with favourable developments in markets and Turkey's credibility.
Some bankers say any deal with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) will strengthen the country's ability to borrow abroad.

Turkey and the IMF are expected to resume talks in late January or early February. The agenda of the IMF talks will be determined after a visit by Turkish State Minister Fehim Adak to the United States next week.
"In the (February) talks we will ask for the IMF support for our economic programme," State Minister Ufuk Soylemez, in charge of the treasury, told Reuters.
However there is no concrete sign that the talks would produce a stand-by accord. Moreover State Minister Sabri Tekir said a stand-by accord was unlikely.
"The present economic conditions in Turkey do not neccessitate a stand-by accord with the IMF," Tekir told Reuters. "We think that the talks would be an exchange of views."
Turkish economy bureaucrats support the idea of reaching a stand-by accord with the IMF while politicians keep their cautious stance.

"A stand-by accord will of course ease Turkey's foreign borrowing. It will increase the confidence in the Turkish economy and bring discipline to the implementation of economic policies," said the economy official.
"But it won't stop our borrowing if we do not reach an accord," he added.
Turkey is expected to service $11.5 billion worth of foreign debt this year -- about $8 billion by the treasury and public institutions.
Recent credit rating downgradings by Standard and Poor's (S&P) and JCR are expected to increase Turkey's borrowing costs in international markets.
Turkish officials say they hope there will be no further rating cuts this year, rejecting rumours that Moody's would soon also cut Turkey's rating.
Turkey has a B rating from S&P and Ba3 from Moody's.
